activities.caption: call the hunger count before the reveal
activities.name: rpUndernourishedEstimate

config.prompt: The world grows enough calories for everyone. How many people are undernourished worldwide (FAO 2023)?
config.why: Around 735 million — with hundreds of millions more lacking reliable power. Abundance existing, access failing: that paradox is the intellectual heart of provision geography.

activities.anchor: Farming types (syllabus 10.1.1) run on one axis
activities.caption: file each farm: who eats the output
activities.name: rpFarmSort

config.prompt: The first axis of every farm — file each case:

items.label: monsoon rice paddies in Bangladesh, family fed first
little surplus at all — the trap the axis names

config.why: Intensity is the other axis: rice paddies yielding three crops a year and battery poultry (intensive) against Australian ranching and Canadian prairie wheat (extensive) — while geography decides the ceiling: soils, relief, growing-season temperatures and, above all, water.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the hunger note
activities.name: rpAccessSpot

config.prompt: One line of this food-security note is wrong — click it:
lines: The planet's croplands already supply well over 2,800 kcal per person per day, before counting livestock and fisheries.
Hunger clusters where poverty, war and broken infrastructure block access.
Adding global output without changing who can buy food would lift most of the hungry out of it.
Export crops can crowd out subsistence ones.
Food-security policy is as much about incomes, storage and peace as about agronomy.
config.correction: Adding global output without changing who can buy food would leave most of the hungry exactly where they are.
config.why: When war hit the Black Sea breadbasket in 2022, prices jumped in Cairo and Nairobi — wheat-importing countries had optimised for cheapness rather than resilience, and the deficits travelled as prices.

activities.anchor: The challenges (10.3) stack on three fronts
activities.caption: pair each lever with its power and its bill
activities.name: rpLeversMatch

config.prompt: Raising supply — pair each lever with its record:

pairs.right: the biggest single lever — roughly 20% of cultivated land producing around 40% of the harvest, and it salinises soil when drainage is poor

pairs.left: the Green Revolution's dwarf wheats and rices
pairs.right: multiplied Asian yields — and brought fertiliser and pesticide dependence favouring farmers who could afford inputs
saved lives in Ethiopia 1984–85, but can undercut local farmers when free grain floods the market — hence buying locally wherever possible
trees planted across the Sahel to push back desertification

config.why: Security against shocks is the newest lesson: monoculture is the standing risk (Ireland's potato blight, 1845 — one crop, one pathogen, one million dead) and concentration the modern one — Russia and Ukraine normally supply around a quarter of world wheat exports.

config.prompt: Before 2022, roughly what share of Europe's imported gas came from Russia?
config.why: Around 40% — and the war in Ukraine turned that dependency into a strategic wound: Europe paid four times historic gas prices, raced to build terminals for liquefied natural gas from the US and Qatar, and shortened its transition timetable in one winter.

activities.anchor: The two syllabus halves are one system
activities.caption: line up the 2007–08 nexus cascade
activities.name: rpNexusOrder

config.prompt: Food, energy and water move together — sequence the textbook cascade:
items: oil climbs above $100, making biofuels attractive
biofuels pull US corn out of the feed market
config.why: Food production consumes around 30% of the world's final energy; energy production consumes water and land; water constrains both — analysts now model all three together, because optimising one at a time is how the cascade happens.

activities.anchor: the demand side is where the leverage hides
activities.caption: true or false — demand's quiet levers
activities.name: rpDemandJudge

statements.s: A kilogram of beef embodies many times the feed calories it returns.
statements.why: Dietary transition toward meat multiplies land and emissions — production method matters more than transport distance.

statements.s: Food waste at retail and household level in rich countries is the equivalent of a large extra harvest.
statements.why: Roughly a third of food is lost or wasted between field and plate — wasted on plates in richer ones, lost in storage and transport in poorer ones.

statements.s: Efficiency standards have quietly done as much for energy security as any power station.
statements.why: The cheapest barrel and kilowatt-hour are the ones never needed — efficiency first, then diversified renewables, storage and grids.

statements.s: Emissions concentrate where energy is burned, extraction damage where it is mined — and the poorest households pay the highest share of income for fuel.
statements.why: Impacts are distributed unfairly: those least responsible suffer the worst air and the highest energy bills.

activities.anchor: usually a minor share of a food's lifecycle emissions
activities.caption: drag the divider — miles vs what's on the plate
activities.name: rpFoodMilesCompare

config.prompt: 'Food miles are the biggest piece of food's carbon footprint' — drag the divider:

before.label: The food-miles story
before.text: Count the air miles and buy local — the distance is the damage.

after.label: The lifecycle arithmetic
after.text: Production, land-use change and refrigeration dominate; red meat carries a footprint many times that of most plant foods regardless of origin — what the food is matters far more than how far it travelled.

config.why: Seasonality and production method beat proximity more often than not — 'eat less meat, waste less, buy what grows well where you are' outperforms 'buy local' as climate arithmetic.
